issues.title: Downtown parking and the resident parking pilot
issues.summary: Since July 1, residents with registered plates park free in pilot zones near downtown while nonresidents pay. The council has spent much of 2026 adjusting rates and parking for downtown workers, and gets its first data on the pilot on Oct 26.
points: Aug 17: raising downtown on-street rates to $3 an hour for 3 hours, then $6, failed 3-5. Yes: Moreau, Hopkins, Bagley. No: Kelley, Cook, Flynn, Blalock, McEachern.

Sept 14: resident rates stay at $1.25 an hour for the first 3 hours (8-0). The nonresident increase to $3 and $6 has no recorded final vote in the minutes; the city's RAPP page now lists $3 an hour for nonresidents.
Sept 14: Parrott Avenue from Roger Street to Richards Avenue came out of the pilot, with 4 hours free, 5-3 on a roll call.
Sept 28: downtown workforce parking opened to more downtown workers until March 1, 2027 (7-0).
A Shuttle Loop and Public Transit Working Group reports back by Jan 29, 2027.

d.title: Passed second reading on moving most parking rules from zoning into site plan review
d.detail: Parking requirements for most projects (not one- and two-family homes) would be handled through Planning Board site plan review instead of a conditional use permit under the Zoning Ordinance. Councilor Bagley said parking requirements should be eliminated instead. Third and final reading is set for October 26.

d.title: Renewed valet licenses for Portwalk and the Parade Residence Hotel
d.detail: Two separate unanimous votes renewed annual valet license agreements with LAZ Parking Limited, LLC for Portwalk HI, LLC and for Parade Residence Hotel, LLC.

d.title: Accepted and adopted the Housing Action Plan
d.detail: Planning Director Peter Britz presented the plan's action items, zoning actions and incentives, and four residents spoke at the input session. Councilors said more work is needed, citing slow timelines, rents, parking and the lack of federal money for public housing. Councilor Tabor will bring ideas raised back to the Housing Committee.
d.review_note: Minutes say the motion was "Seconded by Councilor Moreau," the same councilor who made it. The actual seconder needs to be confirmed, so seconded_by is left null.

d.title: Gave final approval to moving Fleet Street parking to the east side
d.detail: Parking spaces on Fleet Street will move from the west side to the east side.

d.title: Expanded downtown workforce parking eligibility through March 1, 2027
d.detail: Starting October 1, 2026, the Downtown Workforce Parking Program is open to downtown workers in clerical, customer service, administrative and support staff jobs at businesses that previously took part, until March 1, 2027. Councilors discussed hourly versus salaried workers. Councilor Hopkins abstained because a family member works downtown.

d.title: Asked staff for off-peak parking options for downtown businesses
d.detail: Staff will report back in October on parking options for downtown businesses that need off-peak parking during the workweek.

d.title: Removed part of Parrott Avenue from the RAPP pilot
d.detail: The motion takes the section of Parrott Avenue from Roger Street to Richards Avenue out of the RAPP policy, as amended to allow 4 hours of free parking. Councilor Blalock cited recreation programs; Councilor Hopkins raised library and school staff parking. Several councilors said they wanted more data before changing parking on Parrott Avenue.
d.outcome: passed 5-3 on a roll call vote

d.title: Added 4 hours of free parking to the Parrott Avenue motion
d.detail: This amendment to the Parrott Avenue motion provides free parking for 4 hours.
d.review_note: Minutes record "Motion passed 7-1 (Mayor McEachern)" without saying how the Mayor voted. Councilor Tabor is recorded as opposing "this motion" during the debate, yet only one dissent is recorded. Confirm the dissenter against the video.

d.title: Kept resident parking rates at $1.25 an hour
d.detail: Residents will keep paying $1.25 an hour for the first 3 hours and $2.25 an hour after that for on-street and lot parking in FY2027.

d.title: Considered raising nonresident parking to $3 and $6 an hour starting October 1
d.detail: The motion would raise the nonresident on-street and lot rate from $2 an hour for the first 3 hours and $5 after that, to $3 and $6. Councilors Cook, Moreau, Hopkins and Tabor and Assistant Mayor Kelley spoke in favor. An amendment setting an October 1, 2026 effective date passed 8-0.
d.outcome: no final vote recorded (amendment for an October 1 effective date passed 8-0)
d.review_note: The minutes record the 8-0 vote on the effective-date amendment but no vote on the main motion as amended. Confirm whether the $3/$6 nonresident rate was adopted.

d.title: Adjusted the downtown workforce parking program
d.detail: Changes to the RAPP policy remove the 35 cent transaction fee for workforce parking on Parrott Avenue, raise Foundry Garage workforce stickers from 10 to 12 hours, raise monthly stickers from 20 to 26, and define eligible workers as small business owners and employees of downtown restaurant, hospitality, retail and personal service businesses.

d.title: Limited the Parrott Avenue Lot to residents and downtown workers, at no charge
d.detail: The RAPP policy now limits the Parrott Avenue Lot to resident and downtown workforce parking, with a few spaces set aside for Portsmouth District Court defendants. An amendment to charge no fee passed 8-0 before the final vote.

d.title: Created a Shuttle Loop and Public Transit Working Group
d.detail: The time-limited group will pull together existing studies and data on expanding public transit and report back by January 29, 2027 with a recommended pilot or a design scope for a consultant. Councilor Blalock called it unrealistic; Councilor Tabor noted state law allows parking money to fund transit.

d.title: Passed first reading on moving most parking rules from zoning into site plan review
d.detail: Parking requirements for most projects (not one- and two-family homes) would move from the Zoning Ordinance to the Planning Board's Site Plan Review Regulations. Two amendments passed 8-0: striking "and loading zones" from Section 10.232.38 and striking Section 10.244.50 on conditional use permit conditions. Public hearing and second reading are set for October 13.

d.title: Passed second reading to move Fleet Street parking to the east side
d.detail: Staff explained the contraflow bike lane, sidewalks and ADA access, with construction possibly in late fall and early spring. Three people spoke at the hearing. Third reading is set for September 28.

d.title: Rejected raising downtown parking to $3 an hour for 3 hours, then $6 an hour
d.detail: The proposal would have set FY2027 on-street and lot parking rates. After 12 public speakers, many focused on downtown workers, councilors discussed signage, workforce parking, street versus garage pricing and timing. Several, including the Mayor, said they needed more time and a better plan for workforce parking and for parking revenue.

d.title: Agreed to reconsider the parking rate vote on September 14
d.detail: Assistant Mayor Kelley asked for data from the parking work session to help with reconsideration. The City Manager suggested a report back on September 14.

d.title: Passed first reading to move Fleet Street parking to the east side and make the street one-way
d.detail: Two unanimous votes: one moves parking spaces from the west to the east side of Fleet Street, and one makes Fleet Street one-way from Congress Street to Hanover Street. Councilors discussed effects on outdoor dining, wider sidewalks and a contraflow bike lane (a bike lane running against car traffic). Hearings and second reading are set for September 14.

d.title: Adopted the annual traffic and parking omnibus ordinance
d.detail: The ordinance makes permanent changes to 15-minute parking, no-parking areas and limited-hours loading zones. No one spoke at the hearing. The Council passed second reading, suspended its rules and passed third and final reading. Assistant Mayor Kelley was out of the room for the final votes.

d.title: Amended the proposed downtown parking rates to $3 and $6 an hour, then continued the hearing
d.detail: The amended motion would set FY2027 on-street and lot parking at $3 an hour for the first 3 hours and $6 an hour after that, with no change to resident rates. Councilors said the public is confused by several parking changes at once, and two speakers asked that revenue go to transportation alternatives. The hearing was continued, so no final rate vote was taken.

d.title: Scheduled an August 17 work session on parking rates and how revenue is used
d.detail: The work session at 6:00 pm on August 17 will cover higher on-street parking rates and uses of the money. Councilors raised ideas such as a downtown shuttle loop, electronic garage space signs, and involving COAST (the regional bus service).

d.title: Passed first reading of the annual traffic and parking omnibus ordinance
d.detail: The changes cover 15-minute parking, no-parking areas and limited-hours loading zones. A public hearing and second reading are set for August 17, with a presentation on the locations.

d.title: Gave final approval to moving on-street parking fees into the fee committee process
d.detail: No one spoke at the public hearing. The Council passed second reading, then suspended its rules and passed third and final reading. It also scheduled a public hearing on August 3 to enact the fees staff recommended.

d.title: Scheduled first reading to make Fleet Street one-way with a contraflow bike lane
d.detail: Following the Parking and Traffic Safety Committee's recommendation, the change would make Fleet Street one-way from Congress Street to Hanover Street, keep on-street parking, and add a bike lane running against traffic. First reading is set for August 3.

d.title: Scheduled first reading of the annual traffic and parking omnibus ordinance
d.detail: Each year the City makes permanent the temporary parking and traffic rules approved over the past 12 months. This year's changes cover 15-minute parking, no-parking areas and loading zones. First reading is set for August 3.

issues.title: City Hall and police station upgrade
issues.next: Funding in the FY28 capital plan
issues.summary: On Oct 13 the council unanimously accepted the Municipal Building Blue Ribbon Committee's Final Concept C: a phased renovation of City Hall and the police station, estimated at $58.6 million in total. It is the largest building project in the city's plans.
points: June 22: the committee described a nine-phase plan. Councilor Bagley said phases 1 to 5 (the police station) are estimated at $42.2 million and the full project at $58.6 million.
Aug 3: the council approved up to $6.485 million in borrowing that includes design of the police facility and municipal complex (unanimous roll call).
The current capital plan lists $38.3 million for the project; the Oct 13 vote means the next plan (FY28 to FY33) will be updated.

d.title: Chose the final design for the City Hall and police station upgrade
d.detail: The Council accepted the Municipal Building Blue Ribbon Committee's Final Concept C, including revised third and fourth floors and HVAC and electrical upgrades, with a total estimated cost of $58.6 million. The project will be phased and the capital plan (FY28-33 CIP) will be updated. Councilor Cook said the money would come from the existing capital budget.

d.title: Approved up to $6,485,000 in borrowing for City projects, including police station and City Hall design
d.detail: Resolution #14-2026 covers ambulance replacement, building repairs, the Hampton Branch Rail Trail, storm drains, The Creek neighborhood reconstruction, Vaughan Mall restoration, and design of the police facility and municipal complex. Several councilors spoke in support of the municipal building project.
d.outcome: passed unanimously on a roll call vote

d.title: Scheduled a work session on the police station and City Hall renovation plan
d.detail: The Municipal Building Blue Ribbon Committee described a nine-phase plan. Councilor Bagley said phases 1 to 5 (police station) are estimated at $42,215,000 and phases 6 to 9 (rest of City Hall) at $58,634,000. The Council will hold a work session (a discussion meeting with no votes) before the July 13 meeting.

d.title: Approved a farmers' market license with Seacoast Eat Local
d.detail: Seacoast Eat Local may run a farmers' market at the Municipal Complex on Saturday mornings from May 2 through October 31, 2026.

d.title: Made board appointments
d.detail: Jeffrey Cooper, Demi Dubois, Eli Kaynor, Hope Anderson Puzzo and Margherita Giacobbi to the Arts & Cultural Commission; Joshua Cyr and Jason Goodrich (alternate) to the Economic Development Commission; Amy Dutton and Jennifer Merriam to the Cemetery Committee; and Susan Sterry to the Municipal Building Blue Ribbon Committee.

issues.title: Housing Action Plan
issues.next: Zoning changes go to the Planning Board
issues.summary: A city plan of zoning changes and incentives meant to add housing. The council adopted it 8-0 on Sept 28 after Planning Board review and two public input sessions. Councilors said more work is needed, citing slow timelines, rents and parking.

Aug 3: the draft went to the Planning Board, with public input sessions on Sept 23 and 28.
Sept 17: the Planning Board recommended the council accept the plan.
Planning Board work continues on pre-approved accessory dwelling unit plans.

d.detail: The Portsmouth Housing Authority asked for a sewer extension and reimbursement agreement for its Sherburne housing project. Legal, Finance and Public Works will review it and report back. Councilors had asked many questions about the project's financing.

d.title: Asked for a status update on the Sherburne School project
d.detail: City staff, with the Portsmouth Housing Authority, will update the Council on progress, timelines, milestones and challenges for the project.

d.title: Sent the draft Housing Action Plan to the Planning Board and set public input sessions
d.detail: The Planning Board will review it on August 20, 2026. Public information and input sessions are set for September 23 in the Levenson Room at the Portsmouth Public Library and September 28 as part of the City Council meeting.

d.title: Asked planners to look at pre-approved ADU plans from other communities
d.detail: An ADU (accessory dwelling unit) is a small second home on a lot, like a backyard cottage. Planning & Sustainability, with the Housing Committee and Planning Board, will review pre-approved ADU designs used elsewhere to see if Portsmouth can adopt any. Councilor Tabor asked how such plans would fit historic district guidelines.

d.title: Raised nonresident fees at Spinnaker Point
d.detail: New nonresident rates: $575 a year or $50 a month for adults, $300 a year or $35 a month for seniors, and a $25 daily guest fee.

d.detail: Authorizes the City Manager to get a license from CSX, Inc. and an easement (a legal right to use part of someone's land) from 90 Maplewood Avenue, LLC for North Mill Pond stormwater outfall improvements.

issues.title: School buildings
issues.summary: The council has borrowed for elementary school and playground upgrades this year, and the capital plan schedules a large renovation of the Career and Technical Education Center later in the decade.
points: Aug 3: up to $6.5 million in borrowing for school facility improvements, elementary upgrades, playgrounds, paving and roofing (unanimous roll call). Little Harbour School's playground was under construction, with New Franklin next.
Capital plan: $20.1 million for the Career and Technical Education Center and $10.6 million for elementary schools over six years.

d.title: Approved up to $6,500,000 in borrowing for school projects
d.detail: Resolution #13-2026 covers school facility improvements, elementary school upgrades, elementary playground upgrades, and school paving and roofing. Little Harbor School's playground is under construction and New Franklin School is next. Bonds need a two-thirds vote, which was met.
d.outcome: passed unanimously on a roll call vote

d.title: Requested a report on an Elementary School Citizen Day
d.detail: Asks Superintendent McLaughlin to report back on enabling an Elementary School Citizen Day.

issues.title: Prescott Park improvements and a covered stage
issues.next: Staff report back, date not set
issues.summary: In April the council voted to work with the Prescott Park Arts Festival on park improvements, including a covered stage paid for by the Festival. On Sept 28 it asked staff to report back on those plans.
points: April 20: unanimous votes to work with the Festival on a covered stage and to add park maintenance to the capital plan.
Sept 28: report back requested (8-0); Councilor Bagley also asked Legal to report on the Prescott Park trust funds.

d.title: Asked for a report back on plans with Prescott Park Arts Festival for a covered stage
d.detail: The report follows up on an April motion for the City to work with the Festival on park improvements, including a covered stage and related structures paid for by the Festival. Councilor Bagley also asked Legal to report on the Prescott Park trust funds and City contributions.

d.title: Approved Irreverent Warriors hike on August 29 and a Pilates series in Prescott Park
d.detail: Through the consent agenda (routine items approved in one vote), the Council approved the Irreverent Warriors New Hampshire "Portsmouth Silkies Hike" on August 29, 2026 and a FORM Fitness Pilates series in Prescott Park.

d.title: Voted to work with the Prescott Park Arts Festival on a covered stage
d.detail: The City will collaborate with the Prescott Park Arts Festival to plan and start park infrastructure improvements, including a covered stage and related structures, paid for by the Festival. Councilors asked for chances for public input. Four people spoke afterward on this item.

d.title: Asked Public Works to add Prescott Park maintenance to the capital plan
d.detail: After a staff report on Phase 1A of the Prescott Park Master Plan, Councilor Cook first moved to pause the plan after Phase 1A to focus on basic park needs. On the City Attorney's suggestion, she changed the motion to ask Public Works to include Prescott Park infrastructure maintenance in the Capital Improvement Plan instead.

d.title: Adopted the consent agenda
d.detail: Referred to the City Manager: the Peak East Coast 5K and Wellness Summer Series on August 8; Saturday yoga in Prescott Park on four dates; the firefighters' Fill-the-Boot Drive on August 8; and a Reedmor Books and Brews event in the Memorial Bridge parking lot on July 25, 2026. It also included the Public Works active encumbrances report.

d.title: Asked for a report on Prescott Park changes and a privately funded stage
d.detail: Staff will report on changes to Phase 1A of the Prescott Park Master Plan renovations, and how the Prescott Park Arts Festival, working with the City, could privately fund a covered stage and related structures for the long term.

d.title: Moved ahead on a historic marker in Prescott Park
d.detail: The City Manager will negotiate a license for accepting and placing a historic marker. Curtis Herman said he would agree with the city on the location.

d.title: Allowed talks on a Coast Guard Auxiliary boat slip at Prescott Park
d.detail: Authorizes the City Manager to negotiate a lease with the U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary to berth a vessel at the Prescott Park dock, if all slips are repaired before next season.
